pericopes.text: Now behold, I, Jarom, write a few words, according to the commandment of my father Enos, that our genealogy may be kept.

And as these plates are small, and as these things are written for the intent of the benefit of our brethren, the Lamanites, wherefore, it must needs be that I write a little; but I shall not write the things of my prophesying, nor of my revelations. For what could I write more than my fathers have written? For have not they revealed the plan of salvation? I say unto you, Yea; and this sufficeth me.

Behold, it is expedient that much should be done among this people, because of the hardness of their hearts, and the deafness of their ears, and the blindness of their minds, and the stiffness of their necks; nevertheless, God is exceeding merciful unto them, and hath not as yet swept them off from the face of the land.

links.text: And when he had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he saith unto the man, Stretch forth thine hand. And he stretched it out: and his hand was restored whole as the other.

provenance.route: Mark 3:5 + Ephesians 4:18 + Acts 7:51 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “hardness of their hearts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 3:5, and “blindness of their heart” occurs in exactly one, Ephesians 4:18. “Stiffnecked” is spread over nine verses, but “uncircumcised in heart and ears” occurs in exactly one — Acts 7:51 — which is the single KJV verse holding three of Jarom's four members (neck, heart, ears) in one clause. Jarom's “blindness of their minds” moves Ephesians' organ from heart to mind, which is 2 Corinthians 4:4's idiom (“the god of this world hath blinded the minds”).
provenance.significance: The four members are not a KJV list; there is no verse that has them. What Jarom has done is fuse three New Testament indictments into a fourfold catalogue, and all three are indictments of Israel or of its teachers: Mark 3:5, where the synagogue watches to see whether Jesus will heal on the sabbath; Ephesians 4:18, of the Gentiles' alienated understanding; and Acts 7:51, Stephen's charge in the sentence immediately before he is stoned. Read with Acts 7 recovered, Jarom's next clause is the one that matters — God “hath not as yet swept them off from the face of the land” — because Stephen's stiffnecked hearers do not survive their own chapter.

links.note: 'Because of the hardness of their hearts, and the deafness of their ears, and the blindness of their minds, and the stiffness of their necks.' Two of the four members are KJV singletons and each is reproduced with its possessive pronoun intact: Mark 3:5's “hardness of their hearts” (not Matthew 19:8's “your”) and Ephesians 4:18's “blindness of their heart”. The pilot catalogued Mark 3:5 at 1 Nephi 2:18 and again at 7:8, so the phrase is by now the book's own; what is fresh here is the construction, a rhetorical quartet built by taking one organ from each of three sources and supplying a fourth (“deafness of their ears”) that the KJV does not have in that form at all. Recorded at 'high' rather than 'certain' because the composite, not any single verse, is the finding.

pericopes.text: And there are many among us which have many revelations: for they are not all stiffnecked. And as many as are not stiffnecked, and have faith, have communion with the Holy Spirit, which maketh manifest unto the children of men, according to their faith.

links.text: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all. Amen.

provenance.other: “Communion” is a rare KJV word, in three verses only (1 Corinthians 10:16, 2 Corinthians 6:14, 2 Corinthians 13:14), and “the communion of the Holy Ghost” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Jarom writes “Holy Spirit” where 2 Corinthians 13:14 reads “Holy Ghost”; the KJV does use “holy Spirit”, in seven verses, so the substitution is within the KJV's own range and does not point away from it.
provenance.significance: The KJV's one pairing of communion with the Spirit is a benediction — the closing sentence of 2 Corinthians, pronounced over an entire congregation without condition. Jarom turns the benediction into a test. Only those who are 'not stiffnecked, and have faith' have this communion, and what it yields is measured, 'according to their faith'. A blessing that in Paul falls on everyone in the room becomes in Jarom the thing that distinguishes the many from the rest.

links.note: 'And as many as are not stiffnecked, and have faith, have communion with the Holy Spirit, which maketh manifest unto the children of men, according to their faith.' The verse turns on a word the KJV almost never uses. Set beside the stiffneckedness of 1:3, which came from Acts 7:51, the pairing is pointed: Acts 7:51's stiffnecked 'do always resist the Holy Ghost', and Jarom's not-stiffnecked have communion with the Holy Spirit — the same opposition, in the same two terms, one verse later.
links.whyNot: 'Communion' was ordinary theological English by 1829 and need not have come from 2 Corinthians 13:14; the shared material is one noun plus the name of the Spirit, and the syntax is entirely Jarom's.

pericopes.text: And now, behold, two hundred years had passed away, and the people of Nephi had waxed strong in the land. They observed to keep the law of Moses, and the Sabbath day Holy unto the Lord. And they profaned not; neither did they blaspheme. And the laws of the land were exceeding strict.

links.text: But there rose up certain of the sect of the Pharisees which believed, saying, That it was needful to circumcise them, and to command them to keep the law of Moses.

provenance.other: “The law of Moses” runs through twenty-one KJV verses, but the collocation “keep the law of Moses” occurs in exactly one. For the second half of the sentence the KJV has no “sabbath day holy” at all; the nearest wording is Exodus 20:8, 'Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy', whose infinitive Jarom's 'observed to keep' preserves.
provenance.significance: Recover the context of the one verse that says 'keep the law of Moses' and it is the motion of the Pharisee party at the Jerusalem council — the single place in the KJV where keeping the law of Moses is formally proposed and formally overruled. Jarom's Nephites keep it; and six verses later their teachers are found 'teaching the law of Moses, and the intent for which it was given; persuading them to look forward unto the Messiah', which is the council's own answer reached from the other side of the cross. The chapter holds together the two halves that Acts 15 had to choose between.

links.note: 'They observed to keep the law of Moses, and the Sabbath day Holy unto the Lord.' Two clauses, two sources: the KJV's only verse for keeping the law of Moses, and the fourth commandment in its Exodus 20:8 wording. Below any quotation threshold — five words and four — and recorded as an allusion on the rarity of the first phrase rather than its length; Skousen's sixteen-word criterion would not see it.

pericopes.text: And they were scattered upon much of the face of the land; and the Lamanites also. And they were exceeding more numerous than were they of the Nephites; and they loved murder, and would drink the blood of beasts.

links.text: And whatsoever man there be of the children of Israel, or of the strangers that sojourn among you, which hunteth and catcheth any beast or fowl that may be eaten; he shall even pour out the blood thereof, and cover it with dust.

provenance.route: Leviticus 17:10-14 and Genesis 9:4 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Drink the blood” occurs in four KJV verses (Numbers 23:24, 1 Chronicles 11:19, Psalm 50:13, Ezekiel 39:18) and not one of them is a prohibition; the law against blood is always phrased with 'eat', never 'drink'. So the wording is not borrowed. What is borrowed is the offence.
provenance.significance: The charge is placed one verse after the Nephites are said to keep the law of Moses, and it is the law of Moses that it violates — specifically Leviticus 17:13, the clause about a hunted beast whose blood must be poured out and covered. But Leviticus is not the floor. Genesis 9:4 lays the same prohibition on Noah and so on all mankind, before Israel exists. Jarom's Lamanites are therefore not merely outside the Sinai covenant like Gentiles; they are outside the covenant made with the whole human race after the flood. The verse is doing law, not ethnography.

links.note: 'And they loved murder, and would drink the blood of beasts.' The two charges are the two clauses of Genesis 9 in order — 9:4 forbids blood, 9:6 forbids murder — and they are the Noahic minimum, which is also, not incidentally, most of what Acts 15:20 asks of Gentile believers in the chapter Jarom 1:5 has just drawn on. No wording is shared; the link is entirely at the level of which law is being broken, which is why it is filed figural.
links.whyNot: There is no verbal contact whatever, and a reader may reasonably take 'would drink the blood of beasts' as ethnographic invective with no scriptural referent behind it.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they came many times against us, the Nephites, to battle. But our kings and our leaders were mighty men in the faith of the Lord; and they taught the people the ways of the Lord; wherefore, we withstood the Lamanites, and swept them away out of our lands, and began to fortify our cities, or whatsoever place of our inheritance.

And we multiplied exceedingly, and spread upon the face of the land, and became exceeding rich in gold, and in silver, and in precious things, and in fine workmanship of wood, in buildings, and in machinery, and also in iron, and copper, and brass, and steel, making all manner of tools of every kind to till the ground, and weapons of war; yea, the sharp pointed arrow, and the quiver, and the dart, and the javelin, and all preparations for war;

links.text: And Israel dwelt in the land of Egypt, in the country of Goshen; and they had possessions therein, and grew, and multiplied exceedingly.

provenance.other: “Multiplied exceedingly” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Jarom's second verb, 'spread upon the face of the land', has no KJV phrase behind it — “face of the land” is in no KJV verse, the KJV saying 'face of the earth' — and is the Book of Mormon's own standing substitution.
provenance.significance: Genesis 47:27 is the last verse of the Joseph story: Israel settled in Goshen, holding possessions in a land not its own, grown and multiplied exceedingly. Four verses later, at Exodus 1:7-11, the same growth is the reason given for the enslavement. Jarom's chapter runs the identical sequence and runs it fast — prosperity in verse 8, war in verse 9, prophets threatening that the people will be 'destroyed from off the face of the land' in verse 10. The borrowed phrase brings the outcome with it: in the KJV, a people that multiplies exceedingly in a good land is a people about to lose it.

links.note: 'And we multiplied exceedingly, and spread upon the face of the land, and became exceeding rich.' Two words, but they are a KJV singleton and they land on the one narrative in scripture that this chapter is structurally repeating. The Exodus typology is the book's spine from 1 Nephi 2 onward, and this is the point in it that Jarom needs: not the deliverance but the prosperity that precedes the bondage.

links.text: The son of a woman of the daughters of Dan, and his father was a man of Tyre, skilful to work in gold, and in silver, in brass, in iron, in stone, and in timber, in purple, in blue, and in fine linen, and in crimson; also to grave any manner of graving, and to find out every device which shall be put to him, with thy cunning men, and with the cunning men of my lord David thy father.

provenance.route: 2 Chronicles 2:14 (with 2:7, Exodus 31:4, 35:32) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “In gold, and in silver” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Exodus 31:4, Exodus 35:32, 2 Chronicles 2:7 and 2 Chronicles 2:14 — and every one of them is a craftsman's commission. 2 Chronicles 2:14 is the only member of the four that puts timber in the list with the metals, which is what Jarom's 'fine workmanship of wood' requires. Jarom adds two materials the formula never has: copper, a KJV word in two verses only, and steel, in four, three of which are 'a bow of steel'.
provenance.significance: Every KJV occurrence of this catalogue is a commission to build for God — Bezalel for the tabernacle, Huram for the temple. Jarom takes the sanctuary artisan's list and carries it, without a break in the sentence, to 'weapons of war; yea, the sharp pointed arrow, and the quiver, and the dart, and the javelin, and all preparations for war'. The chapter is a colophon by a man who never mentions a temple, and the vocabulary of temple craft has been transferred entire to armament. The added 'steel' points the same way: in the KJV it is almost only ever a bow.

links.note: 'In gold, and in silver, and in precious things, and in fine workmanship of wood, in buildings, and in machinery, and also in iron, and copper, and brass, and steel.' The spine of the list — gold, silver, metals, timber — is the KJV's fourfold craft formula, and the member closest to Jarom's is Huram's at 2 Chronicles 2:14. Recorded at 'moderate': the formula is common to four verses rather than unique to one, and a list of trade metals is the sort of thing that can be assembled without a source.

pericopes.text: and thus being prepared to meet the Lamanites, they did not prosper against us. But the word of the Lord was verified, which he spake unto our fathers, saying, That inasmuch as ye will keep my commandments, ye shall prosper in the land.

links.text: And keep the charge of the LORD thy God, to walk in his ways, to keep his statutes, and his commandments, and his judgments, and his testimonies, as it is written in the law of Moses, that thou mayest prosper in all that thou doest, and whithersoever thou turnest thyself:

provenance.other: “Prosper in the land” is in no KJV verse, and “that thou mayest prosper” occurs in exactly three (Joshua 1:7, 1 Kings 2:3, 3 John 1:2), of which the two Deuteronomic charges are the ones in view; 1 Kings 2:3 has 'that thou mayest prosper in all that thou doest' and Joshua 1:7 'that thou mayest prosper whithersoever thou goest'. The Book of Mormon's fixed form of the promise was adjudicated at 1 Nephi 2:20 and is by Jarom's date a formula of the book rather than a fresh borrowing, which is why the mediation is 'OT-via-earlier-BoM'.
provenance.significance: Jarom does not merely repeat the promise; he says it has been kept — 'the word of the Lord was verified, which he spake unto our fathers'. That is a claim about a text, and it is the reason the chapter can be as short as it is: the promise has already done its work, so Jarom need only report the balance. It is also, in its KJV original, a dying king's charge to his heir. Two verses earlier Jarom has named 'our kings and our leaders'; the promise arrives in this chapter in the mouths of a dynasty, which is where 1 Kings 2:3 put it.

links.note: 'That inasmuch as ye will keep my commandments, ye shall prosper in the land.' The proximate model is not the Bible but 1 Nephi 2:20, where the promise is first given and where the catalogue adjudicates its Deuteronomic wording against 1 Kings 2:3 and Joshua 1:7. Hardy's study edition cross-references this verse to 1 Nephi 2:20 and 2 Nephi 1:20 — an internal recurrence; he gives no biblical row here — and that is exactly the right observation: by Jarom the sentence is quoted as scripture already in force, marked as such by 'was verified' and by 'which he spake unto our fathers'.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Jarom 1.9 (cross-references the promise to 1 Nephi 2:20 and 2 Nephi 1:20; internal recurrence only, no biblical row)

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the prophets of the Lord did threaten the people of Nephi, according to the word of God, that if they did not keep the commandments, but should fall into transgression, they should be destroyed from off the face of the land;

links.text: (For the LORD thy God is a jealous God among you) lest the anger of the LORD thy God be kindled against thee, and destroy thee from off the face of the earth.

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 6:15 (with Amos 9:8) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “From off the face of the earth” occurs in exactly five KJV verses — Genesis 7:4, Deuteronomy 6:15, 1 Kings 13:34, Jeremiah 28:16, Amos 9:8 — and in three of them the verb is 'destroy'. Jarom reads 'from off the face of the land', the Book of Mormon's standing substitution of land for earth, which the KJV never makes.
provenance.significance: This is the second half of the conditional whose first half stands at verse 9. Verse 9 has the Deuteronomic blessing in 1 Kings 2:3's wording — keep the commandments, prosper in the land; verse 10 has the Deuteronomic curse in Deuteronomy 6:15's — fall into transgression, be destroyed from off it. The chapter carries the blessing and the curse in their KJV clothes, in the KJV's order, one verse apart, and puts the curse in the mouths of prophets, which is where Deuteronomy 18 said it would be.

links.note: 'That if they did not keep the commandments, but should fall into transgression, they should be destroyed from off the face of the land.' Of the five KJV verses with this clause, Deuteronomy 6:15 is the one that is a conditional threat to a covenant people in a land they have been given, which is Jarom's situation exactly; Amos 9:8 supplies the same words for a 'sinful kingdom' and, like Jarom's verse 3 ('hath not as yet swept them off'), holds back from utter destruction.

pericopes.text: wherefore, the prophets, and the priests, and the teachers, did labor diligently, exhorting, with all long suffering, the people to diligence; teaching the law of Moses, and the intent for which it was given; persuading them to look forward unto the Messiah, and believe in him to come, as though he already was. And after this manner did they teach them.

links.text: Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.

provenance.other: “With all longsuffering” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 1830 prints it as two words, 'long suffering', set off by commas; 1920 closed the commas and hyphenated it to 'long-suffering'. The KJV compound is one word, so the editorial drift is away from the source's orthography in both editions — the reverse of the 1 Nephi 1:20 case, where 1920 corrected back toward the KJV (CONVENTIONS §8).
provenance.significance: 2 Timothy 4:2 is Paul's charge to a minister: 'Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.' Jarom hands the charge to an institution — 'the prophets, and the priests, and the teachers' — keeps 'exhort' and the singleton phrase, and then in the very next verse supplies the object the charge began with: 'they did prick their hearts with the word'. The word Timothy is told to preach is the word Jarom's teachers prick with, and the two halves of 2 Timothy 4:2 are distributed across two consecutive Nephite verses.

links.note: 'Did labor diligently, exhorting, with all long suffering, the people to diligence.' The verb and the adverbial phrase are both Paul's, and the phrase is a KJV singleton. The clause that follows — 'teaching the law of Moses, and the intent for which it was given; persuading them to look forward unto the Messiah' — is Galatians 3:24's schoolmaster in different words: the law's purpose is to bring its keepers to Christ. Nothing verbal is shared with Galatians, and it is entered as a composite rather than a separate row for that reason; “the law was our schoolmaster” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and Jarom reproduces none of it.

links.text: (As it is written, I have made thee a father of many nations,) before him whom he believed, even God, who quickeneth the dead, and calleth those things which be not as though they were.

provenance.other: “As though they were” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Job 39:16 and Romans 4:17; only Romans 4:17 uses the construction of a thing believed before it exists.
provenance.significance: Romans 4 is the KJV's argument about believing a promise before its fulfilment: Abraham, 'who against hope believed in hope', before a God 'who quickeneth the dead, and calleth those things which be not as though they were'. That is precisely the pedagogical problem Jarom's teachers are solving — how a people under the law of Moses is to have faith in a Messiah who has not come. The Book of Mormon's standing answer is to speak of the future Christ in the past tense, and this verse states the rule for it in Paul's own grammatical figure.

links.note: 'Persuading them to look forward unto the Messiah, and believe in him to come, as though he already was.' The contact is three common words and a tense-play, so this is filed as an echo, not an allusion — but the tense-play is the point of both sentences, and Romans 4:17 is the only KJV verse where calling a thing that is not 'as though' it were is a description of faith rather than of an ostrich.
links.whyNot: 'As though' is ordinary English and the agreement runs to three words; Job 39:16 shows the phrase is nobody's property. A reader who declines this loses nothing from the chapter's other rows.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that by so doing, they kept them from being destroyed upon the face of the land: for they did prick their hearts with the word, continually stirring them up unto repentance.

links.text: Now when they heard this, they were pricked in their heart, and said unto Peter and to the rest of the apostles, Men and brethren, what shall we do?

provenance.other: “Pricked in their heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The verb is used of the heart nowhere else in the KJV; Psalm 73:21's 'I was pricked in my reins' is the only near neighbour.
provenance.significance: Acts 2:37 is the crowd's response to the first Christian sermon: pricked in the heart, they ask 'Men and brethren, what shall we do?', and Peter answers in the next verse, 'Repent'. Jarom compresses the whole exchange into a single clause — pricking, and then repentance — and inverts its grammar on the way. In Acts the hearers are pricked; in Jarom the teachers do the pricking, 'with the word', which is the instrument 2 Timothy 4:2 named one verse earlier. And what in Acts is one event on one day becomes in Jarom an institution: 'continually', across the two hundred and thirty-eight years verse 13 then counts.

links.note: 'For they did prick their hearts with the word, continually stirring them up unto repentance.' A KJV singleton reproduced with its noun and its possessive, turned from passive to active. Taken with 1:11 the pair is a small system: 2 Timothy 4:2 supplies the charge and the word to be preached, Acts 2:37-38 supplies what preaching it does to hearers and what they are to do about it — the two consecutive verses draw on the New Testament's charge to preachers and its model of a congregation's response, in that order.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that two hundred and thirty and eight years had passed away, after the manner of wars, and contentions, and dissentions, for the space of much of the time.

And I, Jarom, do not write more, for the plates are small.—But behold, my brethren, ye can go to the other plates of Nephi: for behold, upon them the record of our wars are engraven, according to the writings of the kings, or that which they caused to be written.

links.text: And the rest of the acts of Jeroboam, how he warred, and how he reigned, behold, they are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.

provenance.route: the Deuteronomistic source-citation formula (1 Kings 14:19 and thirty-three parallels) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The formula 'are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings' runs through thirty-four KJV verses in 1-2 Kings, far too many to identify one; 1 Kings 14:19 is cited as the first occurrence and the one that names warfare ('how he warred'), which is what Jarom's version records. Separately, “engraven” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 3:7, of the law written and engraven in stones — the KJV's only use of the word for a text cut into a hard surface, which is Jarom's whole subject.
provenance.significance: Jarom's colophon reproduces the shape of the Deuteronomistic historian's source note, with both of its distinctive elements intact: a fuller record kept elsewhere, and warfare as the thing that record contains. The formula in Kings exists to say that the compiler has abridged and that the archive is a royal one; Jarom says exactly that — 'according to the writings of the kings, or that which they caused to be written'. What is unusual is who is speaking. In Kings the formula is the narrator's; here it belongs to a man who has just declined to write his own prophecies because 'the plates are small', so the ancient device for pointing past a summary is being used to justify a summary of one page.

links.note: 'Ye can go to the other plates of Nephi: for behold, upon them the record of our wars are engraven, according to the writings of the kings.' No wording is reproduced, which is why this is filed figural; the link is at the level of the form. 1830's 'the record of our wars are engraven' has a singular noun with a plural verb and 1920 regularized it to 'records' (CONVENTIONS §8) — as at 1 Nephi 1:20, the first edition is the rougher and the later edition the tidier text, and the direction of the change is worth recording.

pericopes.text: And I deliver these plates into the hands of my son Omni, that they may be kept according to the commandments of my fathers.
